Why Jain Diwali Is a Celebration and a Farewell: The Story of Bhagwan Mahavir's Last Night
For Jains, Diwali began with a farewell.For them, the festival is as much about remembering as it is about celebrating
For Jains, Diwali began with a farewell. For them, the festival is as much about remembering as it is about celebrating.
Most of us grew up with one version of the Diwali story. Jain families grow up with another, and it starts on a moonless night more than 2,500 years ago, in the alms hall of a king named Hastipal, in a town called Pavapuri (currently in Bihar)
Bhagwan Mahavir, the 24th Tirthankara, had been teaching for close to two days without a break. Jain tradition puts his final discourse at sixteen prahars, beginning on Dhanteras and ending on Diwali. When it was over, he emerged from the Samavasaran, the great assembly where Tirthankaras teach, and went to Hastipal's hall, where people kept coming for a last darshan.
He knew his time had come. He also knew that one person in particular would find it hard.
Gautam Swami was his chief disciple. The love that Gautam had for Bhagwan Mahavir had become the one thing still holding him back from Kevaljnan, the state of complete knowledge. So he sent him away. There was a Brahmin named Devsharma in a nearby village, he told Gautam, who would find spiritual awakening through him. Gautam went at once. "As You command, Lord," he said.
It was a kindness that would only make sense later.
That night, the new-moon night of the month of Aso, Bhagwan Mahavir slowly withdrew from the world. The traditional account is precise about it. First he stilled the outward workings of mind and speech, then the subtlest movements of the body, then the subtle workings of speech and mind. He entered the last stage of pure meditation, Shukla Dhyan, in which all activity ends. It lasted as long as it takes to say five short syllables. Then he was liberated, and ascended to Moksh, completely free from karmic bondage and the cycles of birth and death.
When the kings heard, they lit lamps. The light of their lives had gone out, the account says, and they wanted to mark it. People have lit diyas on that night ever since.
A festival with a lump in its throat.
This is why Jain Diwali feels a little different from the noise outside. It celebrates the highest thing a soul can reach. It also remembers the day his followers lost their teacher.
Pujya Gurudevshri Rakeshji, who founded Shrimad Rajchandra Mission Dharampur (SRMD) in 1994, often explains this with an image every Indian family will recognise. Think of a daughter's wedding, he says. There is joy all day. And then the car pulls away, and the same family is in tears. Nobody thinks that strange. Diwali, for a Jain seeker, is something like that.
What Gautam did

Rishabhanatha (Devanagari: ऋषभनाथ), also known as Rishabhadeva (Devanagari: ऋषभदेव, Ṛṣabhadeva), Rishabha (Devanagari: ऋषभ, Ṛṣabha) or Ikshvaku (Devanagari: इक्ष्वाकु, Ikṣvāku), is the legendary first tirthankara (Supreme preacher) of Jainism.[7][8] He was the first of twenty-four teachers in the present half-cycle of time in Jain cosmology and is called a "ford maker" because his teachings helped one cross the sea of interminable rebirths and deaths. He was the spiritual successor of Sampratti Bhagwan, the last Tirthankara of the previous time cycle.[6][9] He is also known as Ādinātha (lit. 'first Lord'),[9] as well as Aadishvara (first Jina), Yugadideva (first deva of the yuga), Prathamarajeshwara (first God-king) and Nabheya (son of Nabhi).[10][11] He is also known as Ikshvaku, establisher of the Ikshvaku dynasty. He attracts most devotional worship among Jains long with Mahavira, Parshvanatha, Neminatha and Shantinatha. He is regarded as the father of human civilization. He organized the human society into three occupation based proto-groups namely kshatriya (rulers), aryya (merchants and traders) and sukshma (specialized skilled workers).[12] His son Bharata Chakravarti became the first kshatriya and the universal monarch after whom India was named Bhāratavarsha or Bhārat.[13]Hinduism’s Bhagavata Purana claim him as an avatar of Vishnu.[13] Jains consider him as an entirely distinct, fully enlightened human being who attained salvation. Rishabhanatha is one of the five Tirthankaras that attract the most devotional worship among the Jains.[14]
According to traditional accounts, many millions of years ago, he was born to king Nabhi and queen Marudevi in the north Indian city of Ayodhya, also called Vinita.[6] He had two wives, Sumangalā and Sunandā. Sumangalā is described as the mother of his ninety-nine sons (including Bharata) and one daughter, Brahmi. Sunandā is depicted as the mother of Bahubali and Sundari. The sudden death of Nilanjana, one of the dancers sent by Indra to perform in his courtroom, reminded him of the world's transitory nature, and he developed a desire for renunciation.
After his renunciation, the legends as described in major Jain texts such as Hemachandra's Trishashti-Shalakapurusha-Charitra and Adinathcharitra written by Acharya Vardhamansuri states that Rishabhanatha travelled without food for 400 days.[15][16][17] The day on which he got his first ahara (food) is celebrated by Jains as Aksha

SOURCE thejainreligion.in (Rishabhanatha (Adinatha) | First Tirthankara of Jainism):
According to Jain tradition, Rishabhanatha was born to King Nabhi and Queen Marudevi in the ancient city of Ayodhya (also called Vinita), the capital of the Ikshvaku dynasty. He is said to have had two wives, Sumangala and Sunanda, and many children, including his sons Bharata and Bahubali, who feature prominently in later Jain narratives.
Jain texts describe him as the one who guided early human society away from a primitive state of nature by teaching essential arts and skills: agriculture, pottery, writing, weaving, and other crafts, as well as the organization of society into occupational groups. For this reason he is often regarded as a civilizational figure, distinct from the other Tirthankaras whose accounts are more purely spiritual and symbolic.
After ruling as a king, he renounced worldly life, undertook rigorous asceticism, and attained kevala jnana (omniscient knowledge), becoming a Tirthankara — a "ford-maker" who shows others the path across the cycle of rebirth. His life is recounted in detail in the Adi Purana, a major Jain text composed by Acharya Jinasena.
Rishabhanatha's era belongs to the vast, cyclical time-scale of Jain cosmology, placing him far beyond the reach of conventional historical dating, yet Jains regard him as a real and foundational figure whose teachings shaped the moral and social order.
Like all Tirthankaras, Rishabhanatha taught the path of ahimsa (non-violence), right conduct, and renunciation leading to liberation, while also being credited with establishing the practical foundations of civilized life.

SOURCE en.wikipedia.org (Tirthankara - Wikipedia):
In Jainism, a Tirthaṅkara (IAST: tīrthaṅkara; lit. 'ford-maker') is a saviour and supreme preacher of the dharma (righteous path).[1] The term refers to one who establishes a tirtha,[2] a fordable passage across saṃsāra, the sea of interminable birth and death. According to Jains, tirthaṅkaras are the supreme preachers of dharma, who have conquered saṃsāra on their own and established a path for others to follow.[3] After understanding the true nature of the self or soul, the Tīrthaṅkara attains kevala jnana (omniscience). A Tirthaṅkara provides a bridge for others to follow from saṃsāra to moksha (liberation).[4]
In Jain cosmology, the wheel of time is divided into two halves, Utsarpiṇī, the ascending time cycle, and Avasarpiṇī, the descending time cycle, of which the latter is the current cycle. In each half of the cycle, exactly 24 tirthaṅkaras are said to appear in this part of the universe. There have been infinitely many tirthaṅkaras in the past.[5] The first tirthaṅkara in the present cycle (Hunda Avsarpinī) was Rishabhanatha, who is credited with formulating and organising humans to live in a society harmoniously. The 24th and last tirthaṅkara of the present half-cycle is traditionally identified as Mahavira (599 BCE–527 BCE).[6][7][8] History records the existence of Mahavira and his predecessor, Parshvanatha, the 23rd tirthaṅkara in the 9th century BCE.[9]
A tirthaṅkara organises the sangha, a fourfold order comprising male and female monastics, śrāvakas (male followers) and śrāvikās (female followers).[10]
The teachings of a tirthaṅkara form the basis for the Jain canons. The inner knowledge of a tirthaṅkara is believed to be perfect and identical in every respect, and their teachings contain no contradictions. The degree of elaboration varies according to the level of society's spiritual advancement and purity during the tirthaṅkara's period of leadership. The higher the level of society's spiritual advancement and purity of mind, the lower the elaboration required.
While Jains document and revere tirthaṅkaras, their grace is said to be available to all living beings regardless of religion.[11]
Tīrthaṅkaras are arihants who, after attaining kevala jñāna (pure infinite knowledge),[12] preach the dharma. An Arihant is also called a Jina (victor), meaning one who has conquered inner enemies such as anger, attachment, pride, and greed.[4] They dwell exclusively within the realm of their soul and are entirely free of kashayas, inner passions, and personal desires. As a result of this, unlimited siddhis, or spiritual powers, are readily available to them, which they use exclusively for the spiritual elevation of living beings. Through darśana, divine vision, and deshna, divine speech, they help others attain kevalajñana and moksha (final liberation).
The word tirthaṅkara signifies the founder of a tirtha, a fordable passage across saṃsāra, the sea of interminable births and deaths.[13][14][15][16] Tīrthaṅkaras are variously called "Teaching Gods", "Ford-Makers", "Crossing Makers", and "Makers of the River-Crossing".[17][16]
Academic and historical consensus broadly accepts Parshvanatha (c. 8th century BCE) and Mahavira (c. 6th century BCE) as historical figures.[18][19] Parshvanatha, the 23rd tirthaṅkara, is understood as a predecessor who preached the "fourfold restraint" (chaturyama dharma).[20][21] Mahavira is seen as a restorer of Jaina Dharma[22]. In Jain tradition, the first great spiritual teacher of the present cosmic age is Rishabhanatha, also called Adinatha, "the first lord." He is the first of the twenty-four Tirthankaras, beings who cross the ocean of birth and death and show others the way across it. His life is recorded most fully beginning at Parva 1 (the first of its books, parva meaning a book or section of a long epic) of the Adipurana, a forty-two-parva epic begun by the Digambara (a major Jain monastic tradition) monk Jinasena and completed after his death by his disciple Gunabhadra. Tradition places his life at a time so distant it is measured in countless ages, when human beings still lived as simply as the animals around them.
Teacher of Civilization
In the beginning, the Adipurana recounts, people lived content as children of nature, eating wild fruit and leaves, sleeping beneath trees, without farming, weaving, or shelter of their own making. Rishabhanatha, seeing their helplessness, taught them how to till the land, spin cloth from cotton and wool, and build homes that could withstand the weather. He is credited with teaching them tools, cooking, and the arts. Alongside these crafts, he set out the first principles of organized society: property, honest trade, and the rule of law. For these gifts, Jain tradition remembers him as the founder of civilization itself, not merely a religious teacher.
The Twenty-Four Tirthankaras
Rishabhanatha stands first in an unbroken line of twenty-four Tirthankaras that Jain tradition holds appeared across this cosmic age, each one teaching the same path of liberation anew for their own time:

A Kingdom and a Family
Rishabhanatha was not born a king, but the people, needing guidance, made him one. He ruled for many years, seeing that his subjects had what they needed to live well. Tradition names two wives, Sumangala and Sunanda. Among his many children, two sons and two daughters stand out in the record. Bharata, his eldest son, became a great emperor and gave his name to Bharata, the traditional name for India still used in scripture today. Bahubali, a second son, is remembered for his own extraordinary asceticism. His daughters, Brahmi and Sundari, are credited in turn with teaching humanity writing and numerals. Life of first tithankar
The first Tirthankara in Jainism is Lord Rishabhanatha (also known as Adinath). His life, as described in Jain scriptures, is rich with spiritual significance and sets the foundation for Jain philosophy.
Birth and Early Life: Rishabhanatha was born in Ayodhya to King Nabhiraja and Queen Marudevi. His birth is celebrated with great auspiciousness in Jain tradition, and he is often depicted with the emblem of a bull.
Kingship: Rishabhanatha grew up to be a wise and just ruler. He is credited with teaching people various arts, crafts, and ways of livelihood, such as agriculture, pottery, and the use of fire. He is considered the pioneer of civilization and social order.
Renunciation: After ruling for many years and fulfilling his worldly duties, Rishabhanatha renounced his kingdom and all possessions to seek spiritual liberation. He became a monk and practiced deep meditation and austerity (tapasya).
Kevala Jnana (Omniscience): Through intense penance and spiritual practices, Rishabhanatha attained Kevala Jnana (infinite knowledge). After this realization, he began to teach the path to liberation (moksha) to others, thus becoming the first Tirthankara—one who establishes the fourfold Jain community (monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen).
Preaching and Nirvana: Rishabhanatha preached the principles of non-violence (ahimsa), truth (satya), non-stealing (asteya), celibacy (brahmacharya), and non-possessiveness (aparigraha). After a long life dedicated to spiritual upliftment, he attained nirvana (liberation) at Mount Ashtapada (believed by some to be Mount Kailash).
Significance: Lord Rishabhanatha is revered as the founder of Jain tradition and the first to establish the spiritual path that all Tirthankaras and followers of Jainism have since followed.
His teachings emphasize self-restraint, compassion, and the pursuit of spiritual knowledge as the means to ultimate liberation.
